elements.char: Summary
elements.label: text

elements.char: Our final model, the attractant+repellent model, appeared to reproduce the main features of
elements.label: text

elements.char: L1 aggregation. Spectral analysis suggests that the spatial patterning of aggregates in simula-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tions resembles experimental results, although further work along these lines will be necessary.
elements.label: text

elements.char: This model is minimal, we believe, in the sense that no simpler model of the Keller-Segel form
elements.label: text

elements.char: can adequately reproduce the experimentally observed behavior. In particular, the observed
elements.label: text

elements.char: patterning of aggregates—their roughly uniform spacing and sizes, required a short-range
elements.label: text

elements.char: attractive influence and a longer-range repulsive influence. Luca et. al. [31] similarly conclude
elements.label: text

elements.char: that a two-signal model is necessary to reproduce the patterning of senile plaques in their Kel-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ler-Segel model of Alzheimer disease.
elements.label: text

elements.char: In our model the attractive and repulsive influences took the form of labile diffusible small
elements.label: text

elements.char: molecules produced by the worms. Some other possibilities that can be imagined work equally
elements.label: text

elements.char: well. For instance, the attractant could be replaced by a ubiquitous repellent that is locally
elements.label: text

elements.char: destroyed by the worms. (In some explanations of social feeding, oxygen plays this role.) It is
elements.label: text

elements.char: even possible that the attractant and repellent are the same molecule, if it has the unusual
elements.label: text

elements.char: behavioral characteristic of being repulsive at long range (i.e., lower concentration) and attrac-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tive at short range (high concentration). Either the attractant or the repellent could be replaced
elements.label: text

elements.char: with a physical force, e.g. the physical attraction produced by surface tension (which, however,
elements.label: text

elements.char: has too short a range to work well in our current models).
elements.label: text

elements.char: Validity of the continuum approximation
elements.label: text

elements.char: Two useful approaches to modeling the movements of populations are individual-based mod-
elements.label: text

elements.char: els and continuum approximations. In the individual-based model (also known as a Lagrang-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ian model by analogy to classical mechanics) the population is represented as a collection of
elements.label: text

elements.char: agents, each of which moves and changes state according to its own biological imperatives. In
elements.label: text

elements.char: the continuum approximation (also known as a Eulerian model) the population is instead rep-
elements.label: text

elements.char: resented as a continuous density function of state variables, such as position. As the population
elements.label: text

elements.char: is in fact composed of individuals, the individual-based model has greater
elements.label: text

elements.char: prima facie
elements.label: text

elements.char: validity.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Continuum models, however, are often more tractable numerically and analytically.
elements.label: text

elements.char: We used both approaches but relied most heavily on continuum models. How valid is the
elements.label: text

elements.char: continuum approximation in this case? To what extent does it distort our results? The clearest
elements.label: text
